script.opening: "Hello — Daniel Okafor, I’m ringing about my mum, Grace. Before you say you can’t talk to me, please just listen, because I don’t know what else to do. Mum’s memory has been going for a year, properly going, and last month she gave nine hundred pounds to a man who knocked on the door. And — this is the part that’s killing me — I’m moving to Singapore on Friday. The job’s gone too far to pull out. I need this SORTED before I get on that plane."

facts.text: Gradual, steady: repeated questions within minutes, the same anecdote three times a visit, missed direct debits (red-letter gas bill), a saucepan boiled dry twice, getting lost driving back from the garden centre she’s used for 30 years.

Washes and dresses well, cooks simple meals, recognises everyone, plays bridge on Tuesdays ("she loses now, which she never did"). No falls. Mood seems cheerful — "she laughs it off, says ‘my age, darling’."

£900 cash withdrawn over two days for "guttering work" — no work done, no receipt, the man has been back ONCE since and she nearly paid again ("he was ever so polite"). Daniel found out from the bank statement.
If asked: no sudden changes, no falls or head injury, not on new medications, no infections lately, sleeps well, eats well, drinks "a sherry at Christmas". Still driving — short local trips.

Flight Friday, 3-year contract, only child, father died 2019. The guilt arrives in waves: "I’m abandoning her, aren’t I? Just say it." He wants a diagnosis, a care package and the locks changed — in four days.
Told his mother he’s worried, or that he’s calling. "She’d be mortified. Or she’d laugh at me. Mum doesn’t do doctors." No LPA in place — "we never got round to it".

ice.ideas: Dementia — he’s googled it, scored her on an online test, and is "about 90% sure". He’s probably right about the pattern.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — Friday. The real consultation is his guilt at leaving and the fantasy that everything can be "sorted" in four days. Underneath: the roofer coming back while he’s 7,000 miles away, and the LPA they never set up.
ice.expectations: A diagnosis, a care package, and his mother protected — by Friday. Needs converting to: the right process STARTED by Friday, with him plugged in from Singapore, and Grace at the centre rather than bypassed.

cues: "Before you say you can’t talk to me, please just listen" — he’s braced for the confidentiality wall; how you handle the first 30 seconds decides the call.
"I’m abandoning her, aren’t I? Just say it." — the guilt, asking to be either confirmed or absolved; do neither carelessly.
"He’s been back once since" — the roofer is not history; it’s a live, repeating safeguarding risk.

checkpoints.text: Sets the confidentiality rails warmly in the first minute: everything can flow IN; nothing about Grace flows out — and listening to all of it breaches nothing

Takes a proper collateral history and distinguishes the pattern: 12 months of gradual decline with preserved ADLs = memory-pathway territory, NOT delirium — while screening the delirium triggers (drugs, infection, falls) to be sure

Builds the route in WITH Grace at the centre: Daniel tells her openly that he is worried and that he rang; she is invited to a review whose real purpose — her memory — is explained to her, never disguised as a blood-pressure check; the GP does bloods + a validated brief cognitive test + memory-clinic referral with her consent (NICE NG97)

Handles the live risks by name: the returning roofer (bank scam-protection team, trading standards/101, neighbour alerted), DRIVING (must be assessed and DVLA considered if dementia diagnosed — flagged now, handled at the review), and LPA — urgent precisely BECAUSE capacity is likely still sufficient to grant it
Answers the abandonment question with care and honesty: leaving is a fact, abandoning is a choice — and everything in this plan is him choosing not to

Dismantles the "sorted by Friday" fantasy without crushing him: diagnosis takes months; what fits in four days is the conversation with mum, the GP booking, the bank phone call, and the LPA forms started
Keeps Grace a person, not a problem: she laughs it off, she plays bridge, she has the right to be spoken WITH — the plan happens with her, not to her

Closes with the four-day checklist, dated and owned: who tells Grace (Daniel, before Wednesday), the booked review, the bank’s vulnerable-customer team, LPA forms started online, Daniel’s Singapore contact details on file, and the GP’s commitment to ring him after Grace is seen — with her consent

worked.txt: "Daniel — breathe. Here’s how this works: I can listen to every word, and your account is genuinely valuable — what I can’t do is hand you information back about your mum. So pour it all out, and then we’ll build a plan that gets her seen properly. Deal?"

"A year of slow change, bills slipping, the same story three times — that pattern deserves proper memory assessment, and you’re right to push. It is NOT an emergency happening this week, which matters, because it means Friday doesn’t have to be a cliff edge."

"I’ll be straight: ‘sorted by Friday’ doesn’t exist — a memory diagnosis takes months and your mum’s consent. But ‘STARTED by Friday’ absolutely exists, and started properly is worth more than sorted badly. Let me show you what fits in four days."

"The roofer is the urgent bit — he’s been back once and he’ll be back again. Today: ring her bank’s vulnerable-customer team, they can flag the account and watch for cash patterns. Report him to 101 and trading standards. And tell the neighbour you trust — a curtain that twitches is worth more than a camera."

"The power-of-attorney you never got round to — that’s this week’s job, and here’s the hard truth kindly: LPA can only be GRANTED while she has capacity to grant it. The forms start online tonight. If you wait for the diagnosis, you may be applying to a court instead of signing a form."

"You asked me to say you’re abandoning her. I won’t, because it isn’t true — abandoning her would be getting on that plane having told nobody. What you’re doing is the opposite: you’re building the net before you go. Singapore has telephones, Daniel. The son who rings every Sunday and gets a call after every review hasn’t gone anywhere that matters."

f.learning: A third-party memory call runs on the same rails as every third-party call — everything in, nothing out — but the content is a collateral history good enough to triage: gradual decline over a year with preserved ADLs points to the memory pathway, not delirium. The live jobs are protective and time-critical: the repeating doorstep scam (bank vulnerable-customer team, 101/trading standards), driving flagged for assessment, and the LPA window — grantable only while capacity remains. The hidden agenda is Friday: convert "sorted by Friday" into "started by Friday", answer the abandonment question honestly, and keep Grace — who has rights, humour and a bridge club — at the centre of her own story.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG97 — Dementia · GMC Confidentiality (2017) · Mental Capacity Act 2005 · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive
knowledge.summary: A third-party call: listen fully, share nothing about Grace. A year of gradual decline with preserved self-care points to the memory pathway, not delirium. The urgent jobs are protective — the returning scammer, driving and the LPA — and the plan must involve Grace.

points.t: GMC Confidentiality (2017): you should not refuse to listen to concerns from relatives, but you must not disclose information about the patient without consent. Listening breaches nothing; record what was said and that nothing was disclosed.

Twelve months of gradual decline (repetition, missed bills, getting lost on a familiar route) with preserved washing, dressing and cooking suggests possible dementia. Sudden onset, fluctuation or rapid decline over weeks would suggest delirium or another cause needing prompt assessment.

NICE NG97: take a history from the person and someone who knows them, examine, review medicines, use a validated brief cognitive test, and do blood tests to exclude reversible causes before referring to a specialist diagnostic service. A normal brief test does not rule out dementia.

Doorstep fraud with a returning perpetrator is an ongoing risk. Banks have support for customers in vulnerable circumstances; report to police (101) and trading standards. If Grace cannot protect herself, the local authority safeguarding team can be involved (Care Act 2014).

An LPA can only be made while the person has capacity to make it (Mental Capacity Act 2005), and must be registered with the Office of the Public Guardian before use. If capacity is lost first, family must apply to the Court of Protection for deputyship.

DVLA: a person diagnosed with dementia must tell DVLA. Before diagnosis, getting lost while driving is a safety concern to raise with Grace at her review. The GMC sets out when a doctor may inform DVLA if a patient continues to drive unsafely.

Grace living alone, widowed, bridge club, driving; Daniel as only child leaving for three years; no LPA.

Dementia versus delirium, depression, medication or alcohol effects, B12 or thyroid disorder.
Asked about sudden change, falls, head injury and infection; safety-net for acute confusion.
Gradual cognitive decline with preserved self-care — needs memory assessment; not an emergency.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time

Hypertension review at the same visit; kitchen safety; social isolation after Daniel leaves.
Dated plan, contact details on file, consent sought for updates, safety-net for acute change.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.

Idea (dementia, “90% sure”); concern (leaving her, the scammer returning, no LPA); expectation (all sorted by Friday).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.

When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.

model.text: Hello Mr Okafor, it’s Dr Lee. I understand you’re worried about your mum.

Before you say you can’t talk to me, please just listen. Mum’s memory has been going for a year, properly going. Last month she gave nine hundred pounds to a man at the door. And I’m moving to Singapore on Friday. I need this sorted before I get on that plane.

I’m glad you rang, and I will listen to every word. Here’s how it works: you can tell me everything, and it’s genuinely useful. What I can’t do without your mum’s permission is share information about her. So tell me it all, and then we’ll work out a plan that gets her the right help. Is that okay?
model.why: Sets confidentiality boundaries warmly in the first minute

model.text: Okay. That’s fair. Thank you for not just hanging up.
Tell me about the changes you’ve noticed, from the beginning.

She asks the same question within minutes. Tells me the same story three times a visit. A red-letter gas bill — she’s missed direct debits. Boiled a saucepan dry twice. And she got lost driving back from the garden centre she’s used for thirty years.
Has it come on gradually, or were there sudden changes — days when she was suddenly much worse?
model.why: Distinguishes gradual decline from delirium or stepwise change

model.text: Gradual. Steady. No sudden days.
Any falls or knocks to the head, infections, new medicines, and how is her drinking? How does she manage washing, dressing, meals?
model.why: Screens reversible causes and establishes daily function

model.text: No falls, no infections, nothing new that I know of. A sherry at Christmas. She washes and dresses fine, cooks simple meals. Still plays bridge on Tuesdays — she loses now, which she never did.
And her mood — does she seem low or worried?
model.why: Screens for depression as a mimic

model.text: Cheerful. She laughs it off — ‘my age, darling’.
Tell me about the man at the door.
model.why: Explores the financial abuse in detail

model.text: Nine hundred pounds cash over two days for guttering. No work done, no receipt. He’s been back once since — she nearly paid him again. ‘He was ever so polite.’ I found it on her bank statement.
What do you think is going on with your mum?
Dementia. I’ve read up, done an online test with her. I’m ninety per cent sure.
And you mentioned Friday. How are you feeling about going?
model.why: Picks up the Singapore cue and explores the emotion

model.text: Terrible. She’s got nobody else — Dad died in 2019. Three years. I’m abandoning her, aren’t I? Just say it.

I won’t say it, because it isn’t true. Leaving is a fact; abandoning is a choice. Someone abandoning her wouldn’t have rung me four days before a flight. Tell me — what have you talked to her about so far?
model.why: Answers the guilt honestly and moves to what Grace knows

model.text: Nothing. She doesn’t know I’m ringing. She’d be mortified — or laugh at me. And we never got round to the power of attorney.

Here’s my honest view, without discussing her records. What you describe — a year of slow change, bills slipping, repeating herself, while she still looks after herself — deserves a proper memory assessment. It doesn’t sound like a sudden emergency, and that matters: Friday doesn’t have to be a cliff edge.
model.why: Names the pattern appropriately without breaching confidentiality

model.text: So it can’t all be sorted by Friday?

Honestly, no. A diagnosis takes time, tests, and your mum’s agreement. But it can be started by Friday, and started properly is worth a lot. The most urgent thing isn’t medical — it’s the man at the door, because he’ll come back.
model.why: Replaces “sorted by Friday” with “started by Friday”

model.text: So, four things before Friday. One: talk to your mum, openly — tell her you’re worried and that you’ve spoken to me. I’ll invite her in for a check-up, and she should know why. Two: today, ring her bank — they have teams to support customers who may be vulnerable — and report him to the police on 101 and to trading standards. Tell a neighbour you trust.
model.why: Honest route to assessment with Grace; immediate protection from fraud

model.text: I can do the bank today. Talking to Mum… I’ll do it tomorrow.

Three: the power of attorney. It can only be made while she has the capacity to make it — so this week is the time to raise it with her, and the forms can be started online. If you wait, you may end up applying to a court instead. Four: the driving. Getting lost on a familiar road is worth her talking to me about, and I’ll cover it when I see her.
model.why: LPA window and driving safety raised

model.text: Mum will hate giving up the car.

That’s a conversation for her and me, done kindly. When I see her I’ll check her memory properly, do some blood tests for treatable causes, and if needed refer her to the memory service — all with her agreement. If she’s happy, I’ll ask her permission to keep you updated in Singapore. It happens with her, not to her.
model.why: Keeps Grace at the centre and plans consent for future sharing

model.text: If she suddenly becomes much more confused over hours or days, has a fall or head injury, or can’t be woken properly — that’s urgent, same day, or 999 if she’s very unwell. Can you run through the plan for me, so I know I’ve explained it well?
model.why: Safety-net for delirium or acute change with teach-back

model.text: Bank and police today, tell a neighbour. Talk to Mum tomorrow — she knows I spoke to you. You invite her in. Power of attorney this week. You’ll talk to her about the car. And if I’m in Singapore, you’ll ring me only if she says yes.
Exactly. Leave your Singapore number with reception so it’s ready if she agrees. You’re building a net before you go, Daniel — that’s the opposite of abandoning her.
Thank you. I feel like I can actually get on that plane.

social.t: An only child moving abroad leaves Grace without local family. Neighbours, bridge friends and community services become the safety net.
Doorstep fraud often recurs. Bank support for customers in vulnerable circumstances, trusted neighbours and a “no cold callers” approach reduce risk.

legal.t: Capacity is presumed. An LPA (property and financial affairs, and health and welfare) can only be made while the person has capacity and must be registered with the Office of the Public Guardian. Otherwise, a Court of Protection deputyship is needed.
A driver diagnosed with dementia must tell DVLA. GMC Confidentiality (2017) guidance on reporting concerns to DVLA sets out when a doctor may inform DVLA if a patient continues to drive when unfit.
If Grace is unable to protect herself from ongoing financial abuse, a safeguarding referral to the local authority is appropriate.

professional.t: Listen to relatives’ concerns; don’t disclose without consent; record what was said. Seek Grace’s consent at review to share with Daniel.
Grace is the patient. Any assessment happens with her knowledge and agreement — no pretext appointments.

community.t: Alzheimer’s Society and Age UK for information and support; local memory assessment service; trading standards via the Citizens Advice consumer helpline; Office of the Public Guardian for LPA forms.

redFlags: Sudden onset, fluctuating or rapidly worsening confusion — consider delirium or another acute cause
Falls, head injury, new focal symptoms
Ongoing financial exploitation; unsafe driving; kitchen fire risk
psychosocial: Daniel’s move abroad and his guilt
Grace’s independence: lives alone, drives, plays bridge
What Grace knows and how she will react
ice: Concern: abandoning her; the scammer returning; no LPA

playbook.diagnosis: “A year of slow memory change while she still looks after herself deserves a proper memory assessment. It doesn’t sound like an emergency, but there are protective jobs to do this week.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of it as a slow puncture, not a blow-out. We need to check it properly, with your mum, but the things to protect her — the bank, the neighbour, the power of attorney — can be done now.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked if you’re abandoning her. Leaving is a fact; abandoning is a choice — and you’re building a net before you go.”
management.psychosocial: Turn “sorted by Friday” into “started by Friday”, keep Grace involved, and plan Daniel’s contact from abroad with her consent.
sharedPlan: Daniel tells Grace openly; GP invites her for review with history, examination, brief cognitive test and bloods (NICE NG97)
Bank support team, police 101 and trading standards today; trusted neighbour alerted
LPA started while she has capacity; driving discussed at the review
safetyNet: Sudden worsening confusion, falls or head injury: same-day assessment, or 999 if very unwell
Daniel’s overseas contact details on file; updates only with Grace’s consent

pitfalls.intro: This third-party call is failed at the confidentiality wall in the first minute, or later by a doctor who promises to “sort it” and misses the protective jobs that really are urgent.

items.fail: Refusing to talk because there is no consent on file.
items.why: GMC guidance says you should listen to relatives; refusing loses the history and the relationship.
items.fix: “You can tell me everything; I can’t share anything back without her permission.”

items.fail: Discussing her blood pressure, recent visits or medicines with Daniel.
items.why: Disclosure without consent is a probity failure.
items.fix: Talk about the pattern he describes and the process, not her records.

items.fail: Missing the returning scammer, the LPA window or the driving.
items.why: These are the time-critical protective jobs; examiners expect them named.
items.fix: Bank, 101 and trading standards today; LPA while capacity remains; driving raised at review.

items.fail: Replying to “I’m abandoning her” with “no, no, don’t be silly”, or ignoring it.
items.why: Brush-off reassurance doesn’t land; the guilt is the hidden agenda.
items.fix: Answer honestly — leaving is a fact, abandoning is a choice — and show him the plan.

items.fail: Suggesting she be brought in under a pretext.
items.why: It treats Grace as a problem, not a person, and undermines her consent.
items.fix: Daniel tells her openly; the GP invites her with an honest reason.

items.fail: Ending with “we’ll get it sorted” and no dated actions.
items.why: Unfocused plans and no safety-net are standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Four dated jobs, contact details on file, a safety-net for sudden confusion, and teach-back.

timeMap.d: Everything can come in, nothing goes out. Say it warmly, then listen.
Onset and course, examples, daily function, falls, drugs, infection, alcohol, mood, driving, the doorstep fraud.
His idea (dementia); “I’m abandoning her” — answer it honestly; what Grace knows.
Four jobs: tell Grace, bank and 101 and trading standards, LPA while she has capacity, driving at the review.
Acute confusion or falls = urgent. Contact details on file, consent for updates, teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Refuses to listen because of confidentiality, or discusses Grace’s records; suggests assessing her under a pretext; misses the returning scammer; says nothing about LPA or driving; no safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Listens without disclosing; recognises a memory-pathway pattern; arranges a review with Grace’s knowledge; advises on the fraud and LPA; gives a basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: answers the abandonment question honestly; turns “sorted by Friday” into four dated jobs; explains the LPA capacity window; raises driving sensitively; keeps Grace at the centre and plans consent for Daniel to be updated from abroad.

avoid.instead: “You can tell me everything — I just can’t share information about her without her permission.”
avoid.why: Refusing to listen is wrong under GMC guidance and loses the collateral history.

avoid.dont: “Bring her in for a blood pressure check and I’ll test her memory while she’s here.”
avoid.instead: “Talk to her openly first, so she knows why I’m inviting her in.”
avoid.why: Covert assessment undermines trust and her right to consent.

avoid.dont: “Don’t worry, we’ll get it all sorted.”

SCA_MODELS.why: Keeps Grace at the centre and plans consent for future sharing

SCA_MODELS.text: If she suddenly becomes much more confused over hours or days, has a fall or head injury, or can’t be woken properly — that’s urgent, same day, or 999 if she’s very unwell. Can you run through the plan for me, so I know I’ve explained it well?
SCA_MODELS.why: Safety-net for delirium or acute change with teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: Bank and police today, tell a neighbour. Talk to Mum tomorrow — she knows I spoke to you. You invite her in. Power of attorney this week. You’ll talk to her about the car. And if I’m in Singapore, you’ll ring me only if she says yes.
Exactly. Leave your Singapore number with reception so it’s ready if she agrees. You’re building a net before you go, Daniel — that’s the opposite of abandoning her.
Thank you. I feel like I can actually get on that plane.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG97 — Dementia · GMC Confidentiality (2017) · Mental Capacity Act 2005 · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A third-party call: listen fully, share nothing about Grace. A year of gradual decline with preserved self-care points to the memory pathway, not delirium. The urgent jobs are protective — the returning scammer, driving and the LPA — and the plan must involve Grace.

points.t: GMC Confidentiality (2017): you should not refuse to listen to concerns from relatives, but you must not disclose information about the patient without consent. Listening breaches nothing; record what was said and that nothing was disclosed.

Twelve months of gradual decline (repetition, missed bills, getting lost on a familiar route) with preserved washing, dressing and cooking suggests possible dementia. Sudden onset, fluctuation or rapid decline over weeks would suggest delirium or another cause needing prompt assessment.

NICE NG97: take a history from the person and someone who knows them, examine, review medicines, use a validated brief cognitive test, and do blood tests to exclude reversible causes before referring to a specialist diagnostic service. A normal brief test does not rule out dementia.

Doorstep fraud with a returning perpetrator is an ongoing risk. Banks have support for customers in vulnerable circumstances; report to police (101) and trading standards. If Grace cannot protect herself, the local authority safeguarding team can be involved (Care Act 2014).

An LPA can only be made while the person has capacity to make it (Mental Capacity Act 2005), and must be registered with the Office of the Public Guardian before use. If capacity is lost first, family must apply to the Court of Protection for deputyship.

DVLA: a person diagnosed with dementia must tell DVLA. Before diagnosis, getting lost while driving is a safety concern to raise with Grace at her review. The GMC sets out when a doctor may inform DVLA if a patient continues to drive unsafely.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Set confidentiality boundaries warmly; listened fully; took a proper collateral history.
Grace living alone, widowed, bridge club, driving; Daniel as only child leaving for three years; no LPA.
“Before you say you can’t talk to me”, “I’m abandoning her, aren’t I?” and “he’s been back once since”.
Idea (dementia, “90% sure”); concern (leaving her, the scammer returning, no LPA); expectation (all sorted by Friday).
Review with Grace: history, examination, medicines review, validated brief cognitive test, bloods for reversible causes (NICE NG97), then memory service referral.
Dementia versus delirium, depression, medication or alcohol effects, B12 or thyroid disorder.
Asked about sudden change, falls, head injury and infection; safety-net for acute confusion.
Gradual cognitive decline with preserved self-care — needs memory assessment; not an emergency.
Grace told openly; review booked; bank, police and trading standards today; LPA while capacity remains; driving raised; no covert assessment.
Hypertension review at the same visit; kitchen safety; social isolation after Daniel leaves.
Dated plan, contact details on file, consent sought for updates, safety-net for acute change.

social.t: An only child moving abroad leaves Grace without local family. Neighbours, bridge friends and community services become the safety net.
Doorstep fraud often recurs. Bank support for customers in vulnerable circumstances, trusted neighbours and a “no cold callers” approach reduce risk.

legal.t: Capacity is presumed. An LPA (property and financial affairs, and health and welfare) can only be made while the person has capacity and must be registered with the Office of the Public Guardian. Otherwise, a Court of Protection deputyship is needed.
A driver diagnosed with dementia must tell DVLA. GMC Confidentiality (2017) guidance on reporting concerns to DVLA sets out when a doctor may inform DVLA if a patient continues to drive when unfit.
If Grace is unable to protect herself from ongoing financial abuse, a safeguarding referral to the local authority is appropriate.

professional.t: Listen to relatives’ concerns; don’t disclose without consent; record what was said. Seek Grace’s consent at review to share with Daniel.
Grace is the patient. Any assessment happens with her knowledge and agreement — no pretext appointments.

community.t: Alzheimer’s Society and Age UK for information and support; local memory assessment service; trading standards via the Citizens Advice consumer helpline; Office of the Public Guardian for LPA forms.

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This third-party call is failed at the confidentiality wall in the first minute, or later by a doctor who promises to “sort it” and misses the protective jobs that really are urgent.

items.fail: Refusing to talk because there is no consent on file.
items.why: GMC guidance says you should listen to relatives; refusing loses the history and the relationship.
items.fix: “You can tell me everything; I can’t share anything back without her permission.”

items.fail: Discussing her blood pressure, recent visits or medicines with Daniel.
items.why: Disclosure without consent is a probity failure.
items.fix: Talk about the pattern he describes and the process, not her records.

items.fail: Missing the returning scammer, the LPA window or the driving.
items.why: These are the time-critical protective jobs; examiners expect them named.
items.fix: Bank, 101 and trading standards today; LPA while capacity remains; driving raised at review.

items.fail: Replying to “I’m abandoning her” with “no, no, don’t be silly”, or ignoring it.
items.why: Brush-off reassurance doesn’t land; the guilt is the hidden agenda.
items.fix: Answer honestly — leaving is a fact, abandoning is a choice — and show him the plan.

items.fail: Suggesting she be brought in under a pretext.
items.why: It treats Grace as a problem, not a person, and undermines her consent.
items.fix: Daniel tells her openly; the GP invites her with an honest reason.

items.fail: Ending with “we’ll get it sorted” and no dated actions.
items.why: Unfocused plans and no safety-net are standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Four dated jobs, contact details on file, a safety-net for sudden confusion, and teach-back.
